bio.en: Alex Hardiman is Chief Product Officer at The New York Times, leading teams building news, cooking, games, audio, and advertising products, previously CPO at The Atlantic and a product leader at Facebook.
bio.zh: Alex Hardiman 是《纽约时报》首席产品官，领导构建新闻、烹饪、游戏、音频及广告产品的团队，此前曾任《大西洋月刊》首席产品官及 Facebook 产品负责人。

summary.en: Alex describes how impact at the Times is in service of its mission to strengthen an informed democracy, not the other way around, with impact measured in subscribers and even policy change triggered by reporting. She reflects on being at the center of major storms—Facebook after the 2016 election and the Times during COVID—and what product teams can learn from working alongside journalists. The conversation covers the unique dynamics of building product at a mission-driven news organization versus a FAANG tech company.
summary.zh: Alex 阐述了《纽约时报》的影响力如何服务于“强化知情民主”这一使命，而非相反——影响力既体现在订阅增长，也体现在报道引发的政策变化上。她回顾了自己身处多次风暴中心的经历（2016 年大选后的 Facebook、新冠疫情初期的《纽约时报》），以及产品团队与记者协作的体会。对话还对比了在使命驱动的新闻机构与 FAANG 科技公司做产品的不同动态。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: One thing that's really interesting is that our impact and our business goals are in service of our mission, which is to seek the truth and help people understand the world, not the other way around. What it means is that the way that we think about impact is growing a giant subscription business. That business exists to strengthen an informed democracy at a time when people are struggling to understand basic facts and struggling to understand each other. That means that impact for us is growing subscribers, but it's also when a deeply reported story triggers an important policy change or a new law.
turns.zh: 有一件很有意思的事：我们的影响力和商业目标是为我们的使命服务的，使命是寻求真相、帮助人们理解世界，而不是反过来。这意味着我们对影响力的理解是：壮大一个巨型订阅业务。那个业务的存在是为了在人们难以理解基本事实、难以相互理解的时代，强化一个知情的民主社会。所以对我们来说，影响力是增长订阅者，也是一篇深度报道触发重要的政策改变或新法律。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: When you're a product manager, you're involved again in driving specific metrics like engagement or subscribers, but you're also trying to help stories find their real audience in ways that trigger just this whole different side of mission and purpose driven impact. I didn't feel that when I was at a place like Facebook.
turns.zh: 当你是产品经理时，你要驱动参与度或订阅者等具体指标，但你也在帮故事找到真正的受众，这会触发一种完全不同的使命和目的驱动的影响力。我在 Facebook 那种地方没感受到过这个。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, before we dive in, I'd love to get a little bit of background on just your career. I'm curious, what was your career path to becoming the chief product officer at the New York Times?
turns.zh: 好，开始前我想了解一下你的背景。我好奇你成为纽约时报首席产品官的职业路径是什么？

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: Thanks for asking. I've definitely spent most of my career right at the intersection of journalism and tech. I think in hindsight, if you were to ask my family, they probably wouldn't be that surprised, even though for me I was just rolling with it and following what felt like a really interesting set of problems to solve. But when I just look at my family, there is a ton of journalism in our DNA. My grandfather was a news anchor on the West Coast and I really revered him. My great-grandmother, she was pretty amazing. She actually started one of the first TV stations in the Midwest back in the '50s when it was still pioneering territory.
turns.zh: 谢谢问。我大部分职业生涯都在新闻和科技的交叉点。事后看，如果你问我的家人他们大概不会太惊讶，虽然对我来说我只是随波逐流跟着有趣的问题走。但看我的家族，我们 DNA 里有很多新闻。我爷爷是西海岸的新闻主播，我很崇敬他。我曾祖母相当了不起，她在 50 年代在中西部创办了最早的电视台之一，那时还是开拓期。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: For me, one of my first, the dream for me was to try to find a way to build things in the new space. That's how I first ended up at The New York Times. I've had two stints at The New York Times. My first stint was for a decade, from 2000 to 2016, and it was during a really interesting time of pretty big transformation. There's so much to talk about within that decade, but I would say there are two really big things that happened in that moment. The first was really trying to work with the company to shift from being a print first product into a mobile first product. If you go back to 2006 and you think about it, the Times had no mobile presence whatsoever.
turns.zh: 对我来说，最早梦想之一就是找到在新闻领域做东西的方式。这就是我第一次进纽约时报的方式。我在纽约时报有两段。第一段十年，2000 到 2016，那是一个相当有趣的转型期。那十年有很多可说，但我 скажем 两个大事。第一是和公司一起从纸媒优先转到移动优先。回到 2006 年，时报完全没有移动业务。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: Even the iPhone 2G and the App Store didn't come out I think until like 2008. We just really started investing in small mobile use cases, first on the margins and then more and more aggressively until we were just leading with mobile in everything that we did. New journalism formats, new product features, new revenue opportunities, that type of thing. Then, the second big thing that marked my journey at The New York Times was the shift to a direct to consumer subscription model. This was back in 2011, and there was just a lot of skepticism, including from people at The New York Times, about whether or not people would pay for quality journalism.
turns.zh: 连 iPhone 2G 和 App Store 都是 2008 年才出的。我们开始投资小的移动用例，先在边缘，然后越来越激进，直到我们在所有事上都以移动优先。新新闻格式、新产品功能、新收入机会。第二件大事是转向直接面向消费者的订阅模式。那是 2011 年，有很多怀疑，包括纽约时报内部的人，怀疑人们会不会为优质新闻付费。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: We brought in consultants and they said, "Maybe over the course of history it'll get to one million subscribers, if you're lucky." It felt like a really big nervous [inaudible 00:07:27] at the time. But thank goodness it helped make a market for paid journalism, that has really helped a lot of news organizations find new ways to support quality coverage. But after a decade I did what I think a lot of people did, was you look around and you say, "I love what I do, but I would love to go learn how to do product in the context of a product led digital first company." That's when I went to Facebook and I left in 2016.
turns.zh: 我们请了顾问，他们说「也许在整个历史过程中能到一百万订阅者，如果运气好的话。」当时感觉是个很大的赌注。但谢天谢地它帮着开辟了付费新闻市场，帮了很多新闻机构找到支持优质报道的新方式。但十年后我做了很多人做的事：你环顾说「我爱我做的事，但我想去产品主导的 digital-first 公司学做产品。」这就是我去 Facebook 的原因，2016 年离开。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: The timing is actually pretty important in terms of my experience at Facebook, because when I first joined Facebook, I totally left the media space. I was focused on building out a team that was really trying to help micro sellers in markets like India and other parts of APAC, who were coming online for the first time in really low bandwidth areas, and just wanted to sell their goods through social commerce. Really looking at what WhatsApp and Line and other regional competitors were doing. We were focused on business messaging and the interoperability of the Facebook apps from more of a small business perspective. It was really awesome work.
turns.zh: 时间点对我 Facebook 的经历很重要，因为我刚加入 Facebook 时完全离开了媒体领域。我专注于建团队帮助印度和亚太其他地方的微卖家，他们第一次上网、在低带宽地区，想通过社交电商卖货。看 WhatsApp、Line 等区域竞品在做什么。我们专注于商业消息和 Facebook app 之间的互操作性，从小企业角度。是相当棒的工作。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: Then, the 2016 presidential election happened. I had only been there for a couple of months and as has been discussed very widely and reported widely, it was a wild time where there was just so much reckoning around misinformation, disinformation, election integrity, platform responsibility. I went over very quickly to help out on the news front where I led the product and engineering teams and it was really hard, really interesting work. I did that for a couple of years, decided-
turns.zh: 然后 2016 大选发生了。我才去几个月，如大家广泛讨论和报道的，那是疯狂时期，围绕虚假信息、错误信息、选举诚信、平台责任有大量反思。我很快转去帮新闻那边，领导产品和工程团队，非常难也非常有趣。做了两年，决定——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Before we move on.
turns.zh: 继续之前。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: Right after the election.

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, my God. Before you move on, just what was that like? I don't know how one can describe that experience, but what do you think about when you think back to that time?
turns.zh: 天哪。继续之前，那是什么样的？我不知道怎么描述那个经历，但你回想那时会想到什么？

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: I think about wartime product management, right? You're coming in, and I think there was ... What I appreciated about that time inside of Facebook was that there was just this incredible humility that was needed to really understand and first diagnose what was actually happening on the platform, and the approach to content on Facebook historically it was very binary. You basically had content from friends and family and then you had public contents. Public content could come from anywhere. It could come from a reputable news organization or it could come from my younger brother posting something and declaring it to be true.
turns.zh: 我想到战时产品管理。你进来，我觉得那个时期 Facebook 内部让我 appreciate 的是有一种 incredible 的谦逊，真正理解和先诊断平台上到底在发生什么。Facebook 历史上对内容的 approach 很二元。基本就是朋友和家人的内容，然后是公开内容。公开内容可以来自任何地方——可以是可靠新闻机构，也可以是我弟弟发的东西声称是真的。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: What we really tried to do very quickly was try to unpack the categories of public content to say that there actually is something that is factually accurate information, and that requires a certain craft from the journalistic trade. There are ways to really look at what is trusted information, how you make that a little bit more essential and visible to people on the platform, while then reducing things that are at best dubious or at worse truly misleading propaganda. It was really fascinating and really hard just because the platform hadn't been built to think about classification of coverage in that way.
turns.zh: 我们很快试图做的是拆解公开内容的类别，说确实有事实准确的信息，那需要新闻行业的一定 craft。有办法看什么是可信信息、怎么让它更核心更可见，同时减少最好的可疑、最坏的是真正误导性的宣传。这非常迷人也非常难，因为平台不是为那样思考报道分类而建的。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: Let alone to have the right goals and responsibilities and incentives. There was just a ton of work to figure out how to make the platform far safer and far more informative after, I would say, a pretty intense election cycle.
turns.zh: 更不用说有正确的目标、责任和激励。有大量工作要搞清楚怎么让平台更安全、更有信息量，在一场相当激烈的选举之后。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. I was going to ask you about this later, but I feel like you're drawn towards just crazy, wild and crazy center of the storm roles. I guess that one you didn't expect necessarily to become that. I imagine The New York Times has a lot of that, but maybe a quick question there. What have you learned about just living in a world of just constant chaos and stress and urgency, endless urgency?
turns.zh: 对。我本来要后面问你这个，但我觉得你似乎就是被吸引到疯狂、风暴中心的角色。那个大概你没预期会变成那样。我猜纽约时报有很多那种，也许快速一个问题：在一直混乱、压力、无尽紧迫感的世界里生活，你学到了什么？

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: I would say, if you did ask my family and my husband, he would say that I'm always attracted to the more chaotic problems. I just actually think that that's where product people thrive. The idea of being able to take all of these crazy inputs, trying to create a very structured model to figure out, "Okay, what is true? Where do we have conviction? Where do we have questions? What are the most important problems to solve? How do you prioritize? How do you get a team rallied around a shared context in one single goal? These are actually the conditions where product manager, I think, thrive.
turns.zh: 如果你问我家人和我丈夫，他会说我总被更混乱的问题吸引。我其实觉得那是产品人 thrive 的地方。能把所有这些疯狂输入拿过来、建一个非常结构化的模型 figure out「好，什么是真的？我们在哪有信念？我们在哪有疑问？最重要的问题是什么？怎么排优先级？怎么让团队围绕共享上下文和一个目标集合？」这些其实是 PM thrive 的条件。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: For me, just having been in the journalism space for about two decades now, it's just been or the tech space around news, it's just been a constant set of upheaval and transformation. Some things within our control, some things entirely outside of our control, and so I love it. For me, there's nothing else I'd rather be doing than trying to solve these problems in the world at scale. But it does take a certain amount of just grit and resilience, and the ability to really focus on the most important problems in a given moment. Also, the ability to let other things slide when you have to.
turns.zh: 对我来说，在新闻领域或新闻科技领域做了大约二十年，就是持续的剧变和转型。有些在我们控制内，有些完全不在。我爱它。对我来说没有别的事我更想做。但这确实需要一定的韧性和坚韧，能在给定时刻聚焦最重要的问题。也有能力在该放手时让别的滑走。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: But again, I feel like these are core product skills that we look for in terms of leadership and grit, and the ability to drive through really, really tough problems that there's no playbook for, nobody has ever really done before.
turns.zh: 但我觉得这些是我们找 leadership 时看的核心产品技能：坚韧、驱动没有 playbook、没人做过的极难问题的能力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. You said PMs thrive in this. I think some do. Some are like, "No, leave me out of that."
turns.zh: 对。你说 PM thrive 在这里。我觉得有些是。有些是「不，别把我放进去。」

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: I guess that's true.
turns.zh: 我猜也是。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's a metaphor I like to use when I give PM's advice on where to work within a company, which is there's like the Eye of Sauron, which is the number one most important thing to the CEO at that time. My advice is often don't avoid that thing, usually, but work maybe to the side of that because you don't want to work on something that doesn't matter, that's like over in the shire land. You want to be something that matters but not maybe the most important thing. I feel like you're the opposite. You're like, "Where's the Eye of Sauron focused? I'm going to go there and build stuff." That's pretty awesome.
turns.zh: 我给 PM 建议在公司里去哪工作时有个比喻：有个索伦之眼，就是 CEO 当时最重要的事。我的建议通常不是避开它，而是在它旁边做，因为你不该做不重要的、在夏尔那边的事。你要做重要的但不是最重要的。我觉得你相反。你是「索伦之眼聚焦哪？我去那建东西。」那太棒了。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: Awesome, sometimes, I'm sure there are moments too where it would be nice to chill, but I am drawn to those types of problems for sure. This feels like therapy, Lenny. I'm into it.
turns.zh: 棒，有时候，肯定也有想 chill 的时刻，但我确实被那种问题吸引。这感觉像治疗，Lenny。我投入了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Tell me about your mother.
turns.zh: 讲讲你妈妈。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: She's wonderful.
turns.zh: 她很棒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, great. That's the end of that one. I'll let you finish your career overview and then-
turns.zh: 好，好。这条结束了。我让你完成职业概述然后——

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: I feel like we're almost at present, which is I found that there was so much incredible experience that I was able to soak up and lean at a place like Facebook. For me, I really wanted to figure out how to apply that back into organizations that just had more of a classic journalistic mission and purpose, so I went to the Atlantic for a year. They had just been purchased by the Emerson Collective, so it was a really fun moment of just investment and expansion and ambition. We launched their consumer business. Then, I came back to The New York Times in late 2019, right before the pandemic, and I've been there ever since.
turns.zh: 我觉得我们快到现状了。就是我觉得在 Facebook 那种地方有那么多 incredible 经验可以吸收。我真的很想 figure out 怎么把它应用回有更经典新闻使命和目的的组织，所以我去了大西洋月刊一年。他们刚被 Emerson Collective 收购，所以那是个投资、扩张、雄心的有趣时刻。我们 launched 了他们的消费者业务。然后 2019 年底回到纽约时报，就在疫情前，一直到现在。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh my, just your timing is impeccable every time.
turns.zh: 天哪，你每次时机都精准。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: It really is.
turns.zh: 真的是。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I was doing some research on you before this chat and when you came back to The New York Times, there's all these stories about how big of a deal it was. Returns to The New York Times. That must have been something coming back, because you're there for 10 years initially, and then you came back. What was that experience like just coming back to something like that after being away?
turns.zh: 我之前做功课，你回纽约时报时有一堆报道说这是多大的事。回归纽约时报。回来一定很不一样，因为你最初在那十年，然后回来。回来是什么体验？

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: I felt really lucky. When I left The New York Times back in 2016, it was on really, really good terms. It almost felt as like, I'm going on an externship and I really hope that one day I'll be able to come back and just do my job better. Because I do think there's real value in being able to do product in a bunch of different contexts. You're just so much better at pattern recognition, learning how to solve a diversity of problems, learning to work through things. I had a lot of great support when I left, which was really important. I don't think everyone necessarily has the privilege of that support when they exit a company. When I came back, it was just a real moment of excitement. My interview process, I joked with my boss at the time. But it did actually feel more like therapy.
turns.zh: 我觉得很幸运。2016 年离开时关系非常好。感觉像我要去做个外部实习，希望有一天能回来把工作做得更好。因为我觉得在不同场景做产品真的有价值——你模式识别更好、能解决多样问题、能 work through 东西。我离开时有很多支持，这很重要。不是所有人离开公司都有这个特权。回来时真的是兴奋。我的面试过程，我跟我当时老板开玩笑，但确实感觉更像治疗。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: When you've worked with people for a decade before and you go in, the conversation isn't the normal list of interview questions. It's like, "Okay, here's what type of leader you were a couple of years ago. Here are the conditions on the ground now, how do you feel about X? How do you feel about Y? Are you still passionate about solving this? What else have you learned that's going to make you better?" It was wonderful. It was one of the best interview processes because you're talking to a bunch of people who knew what you were like when you were leading as a person at a different point in your career and they're pushing you to be better. I felt like I got the best chance of a lifetime to come back and try to do my job better than I had been able to do it before, and that's pretty cool.
turns.zh: 你和共事过十年的人聊，对话不是正常面试题列表。是「好，你几年前是哪种 leader。现在地面的情况是这样，你对 X 怎么看？对 Y 怎么看？你还热衷解决这个吗？你还学了什么能让你更好？」很棒。是最好的面试过程之一，因为你在和一群知道你不同职业阶段 leading 时是什么样的人聊，他们 push 你更好。我觉得我得到了这辈子最好的机会回来把工作做得比以前更好，这挺酷的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You've been there three years at this point?
turns.zh: 你到现在三年了？

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: Yeah, three years on Halloween, so coming up very soon.
turns.zh: 对，到万圣节三年，快到了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, wow. That's three days from now when we're recording. I wonder when this comes out. I'm curious, at a company like New York Times, which is, I imagine people think when they think product, they think it's the newspaper. At Airbnb we have this challenge where when we talk to hosts, "Here's the product." You're like, "What is your product? Is it our homes?" You have to help people understand, "Okay, when we talk product, we mean the website and app." What do you think of the product at The New York Times? Then, is it a challenge to help people understand, here's what the product team does?
turns.zh: 哦，哇。我们录制时离那还有三天。不知道什么时候出。我好奇，在纽约时报这种公司，我想大家想到产品就想到报纸。在 Airbnb 我们有这个挑战：和房东聊时「这是产品」。你得帮人理解「当我们说产品，我们指网站和 app」。你觉得纽约时报的产品是什么？让团队理解产品团队做什么是个挑战吗？

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: It's a really good question. At the most basic level, I would say that our product is our journalism, which we then marry with a really compelling and useful user experience, in a way that helps people really act on our journalism so that they can understand and engage with the world around them. For about 150 years, our product was pretty simple. It was a printed newspaper, which is still very beloved today, but the UX of the newspaper was, it was a predictable structure. It was a very finite amount of news. It was time bound, which I think is a really lovely thing in terms of setting expectation. It also has the packaging of the newspaper just such serendipity, where you can move across news, opinion, culture, games.
turns.zh: 好问题。最基本层面，我们的产品是我们的新闻，然后我们和一个非常 compelling 且有用的用户体验结合，帮人真正根据我们的新闻行动、理解和参与周围世界。大约 150 年我们的产品很简单：印刷报纸，今天仍很受喜爱，但报纸的 UX 是可预测的结构、非常有限的新闻、时间限定——我觉得这在设定期望上很美好。报纸的包装也有那种偶然性，你可以在新闻、观点、文化、游戏间移动。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: It's a really great bounded product in and of itself. But about 25 years ago, when we started shifting over to digital, the web, and mobile, the world just fully opened up in a way. We just saw this really tremendous disaggregation and distribution of our journalism. We really tried to meet the moment by building a wide array of products in the news space to extend our reach. Our products then, our digital products were our website, our apps, newsletters, we dabbled with a lot in the VR/AR space early on. That was, I would say, the first big extension of our products. When we then pivoted though to a subscription model, it was a really interesting moment where we actually had to take more of a destination first approach.
turns.zh: 它本身就是个很好的有界产品。但大约 25 年前我们开始转向数字、web 和移动，世界完全打开了。我们看到新闻大量解聚和分发。我们试图通过建一大批新闻产品来扩展触达。我们的数字产品是网站、app、newsletter，早期还在 VR/AR 领域试了很多。那是第一波大扩展。当我们转向订阅模式，那是个有趣时刻，我们实际上要采取更以目的地为先的方式。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: It was almost like the beginning of us rebundling all of what we did, but on our own destination again, in digital destination. Because in order to build a really thriving subscription business, you really need a direct relationship with your customer as opposed to just relying on platforms to really distribute your coverage. That's where, again, we really started rebundling the breadth and depth of value that people once found in the Sunday newspaper at digital scale. Now, today, our product bundle includes even so much more than news, which I hope we'll talk about a little bit more later. We've really scaled our products in a bunch of different categories where we feel like we can really help people understand and engage with the world.
turns.zh: 几乎是我们重新打包我们做的一切，但这次在数字目的地上。因为要建一个繁荣的订阅业务，你需要和客户的直接关系，而不只是依赖平台分发。这就是我们开始重新打包人们曾经在周日报纸里找到的广度和深度价值，在数字规模上。今天，我们的产品 bundle 包含远不止新闻，我们晚点聊。我们真的在一堆不同类别里扩展了产品，觉得能帮人理解和参与世界。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: We have cooking, we have games, we have sports, we have Wirecutter, which is a great innovation surface. We're playing with a new audio app all around audio journalism. We have now six fully fledged different product destinations. The next thing for us to do is to really figure out how to put those together into a bundle that really becomes the essential subscription for any curious English speaking person around the world, who really wants to know what's happening and wants to be able to, again, act and engage and make great decisions based on the products that we build.
turns.zh: 我们有烹饪、游戏、体育、Wirecutter，是个很好的创新面。我们在玩一个围绕音频新闻的新音频 app。我们现在有六个成熟的不同产品目的地。下一步是 figure out 怎么把它们放进一个 bundle，成为任何好奇的英语使用者真正想知道世界在发生什么、想行动、参与、基于我们产品做明智决策的必备订阅。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. It sounds like the strategy is a subscription bundle where you just keep bundling awesome stuff into this bundle. It's an obvious thing everyone has, whether you want cooking or games or The New York Times online.
turns.zh: 懂了。听起来策略是订阅 bundle，你一直把好东西打包进去。这是大家都有的东西，不管你要烹饪还是游戏还是纽约时报在线。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: I think that's right. We did this pretty great exercise and strategy projects over the last year. We took a look and we said, "What is the largest addressable market where The New York Times can be truly valuable every single day to a group of people?" What we found was that there are about 135 million people around the world we believe are willing to pay for the type of high quality journalism based products that the New York Times produces, in the categories of news, gameplay, cooking and recipes, sports, which is why we acquired the athletic shopping recommendations and audio. In order for us to really capture as much of that audience and really serve them well, there are really three things that we need to do to make that essential subscription work.
turns.zh: 我觉得对。我们去年做了个很好的战略项目。我们看「纽约时报能每天真正为谁提供价值的最大可触达市场是什么？」发现全世界大概有 1.35 亿人愿意为纽约时报做的那种高质量基于新闻的产品付费，类别是新闻、游戏、烹饪和食谱、体育——所以我们收购了 The Athletic——购物推荐和音频。为了真正抓住那些受众并服务好他们，要做三件事让必备订阅 work。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: The first is we absolutely need to have the best news destination in the world. When you think about the New York Times, we actually have the solar system metaphor where for us news is the sun in the sense that it's why we exist. It is what gives us our brand heritage and reputation. It's what instills trust. It's also where we just have the largest audience when you think about a funnel for our portfolio, and it's also where we just have the most amount of high quality coverage. But then that sun helps you give birth to other satellite planets or products that have a lot of the same DNA. Again, like great trusted journalism, great journalists who just have real expertise.
turns.zh: 第一是我们绝对要有世界最好的新闻目的地。想纽约时报时我们其实有太阳系比喻：新闻是太阳，是我们存在的原因，给我们品牌传承和声誉，建立信任，也是我们最大受众所在、最高质量报道最多。但那个太阳帮你生出有同样 DNA 的卫星行星或产品——可信新闻、有真正专长的记者。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: A great product experience that allows you to really unlock that value distribution reach, and the other ingredients that you would need for successful products to work. We're really focused on building out beyond news products that really help people engage with their passions and life needs that go beyond news. Then, the third thing is what you're describing as the bundle, how do we create a connected family of products that puts all of those things together so that wherever you come into the New York Times, to news or maybe through Wordle, you know that you're having the best experience within that category.
turns.zh: 让你真正解锁价值分发触达的好产品体验，以及成功产品所需的其他要素。我们聚焦于在新闻之外建帮人参与超越新闻的热情和生活需求的产品。第三就是你说的 bundle，怎么创造一个连接的产品家族把一切放在一起，这样无论你从新闻还是 Wordle 进纽约时报，你知道你在那个类别里有最好体验。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: But then you also can quickly experience and discover everything else that we offer. That's the strategy and the vision, and it's a huge ambition. We want to get to 15 million subscribers by 2027. We're just over 9 million today, and I really think we can do it.
turns.zh: 然后你也能快速体验和发现我们提供的其他一切。这是策略和愿景，雄心巨大。我们想到 2027 年达 1500 万订阅者。现在刚超 900 万，我真觉得能做到。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. I actually wanted to chat about goals and how you think about success as a product team. I imagine the north star metric is what you just said, which is subscribers. If that's true, what other goals do you have across teams? Maybe even further, I'm packing a lot of questions into one question, but I'm curious just how your product team looks. How many PMs do you have? Roughly, how do you structure the teams? Then, roughly, what kind of goals do they all have to try and imagine the product team at New York Times?
turns.zh: 太好了。我其实想聊目标和产品团队怎么想成功。我猜 north star 指标就是你说的订阅者。如果是，各团队还有什么目标？也许更多，我一个问题里塞了很多，但我好奇你的产品团队长什么样。有多少 PM？大致怎么结构？然后大致他们都有什么目标，好想象纽约时报的产品团队？

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: Let's start with structure. First, I love this question talking about my team because I love hyping them. They're amazing, and our success is truly only as good as our people. Yeah, it is so true. For us, when we think about our org structure, the way to set that up so that our people can really do their best work is that we have two axis. We have functions and then we have missions. I oversee two functions, which is the functions of product and design. The functions themselves, it's normal of what you would find in terms of functional responsibilities. We focus on standards of craft and excellence, career growth, career frameworks, equitable promotion processes, community of practices, skill development, all of that.
turns.zh: 先从结构开始。我喜欢这个问题因为我爱夸我团队。他们很棒，我们的成功真的只取决于人。对。我们想组织结构时，让人能做最好工作，我们有两个轴：职能和使命。我管两个职能：产品和设计。职能本身和你想的正常职能责任一样。我们聚焦 craft 和卓越标准、职业成长、职业框架、公平晋升流程、实践社区、技能发展等。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: But missions is where a lot of the work happens. These are cross-functional teams, very similar to what we had at a place like Facebook. These cross-functional teams are led by usually a general manager, a product leader, or an engineering leader. They're all pursuing the same high level goals and objectives. Cross-functional missions at the Times, it can include a lot of the same skill sets that you would find at a tech company, PMs, engineers, designers, data scientists, researchers, product marketers. But the big difference is we also have editors, if it's a product space that directly shapes our journalism. I can talk more about that because it's a pretty interesting differentiating factor.
turns.zh: 但使命才是大量工作发生的地方。这些是跨职能团队，和 Facebook 那种很像。通常由总经理、产品 leader 或工程 leader 带领。都追求同样的高层目标和目的。纽约时报的跨职能使命可以包含你在科技公司找到的同样技能——PM、工程师、设计师、数据科学家、研究员、产品营销。但大区别是我们还有编辑，如果是直接塑造新闻的产品空间。我可以多说因为这是个相当有趣的差异化因素。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, that's super interesting. There's a journalist within cross-functional product teams?
turns.zh: 对，超有趣。跨职能产品团队里有记者？

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: Exactly. But we have three different types of missions. We have consumer missions, we have monetization missions, and we have platform missions. Editors are embedded within consumer missions. Those are the missions that I oversee, where we're focused on creating really great products, again, in categories like news, cooking, games, audio, et cetera. That is where having editors involved, particularly like editors who are very product minded, it brings in the best of their expertise and marries it with a lot of the normal signal that you look for in terms of data research and other insights. When you're trying to make sure that you understand a consumer problem and that you're really finding the best creative solution for it.
turns.zh: 对。但我们有三种不同使命：消费者使命、变现使命、平台使命。编辑嵌入在消费者使命里。那些是我管的，聚焦于在新闻、烹饪、游戏、音频等类别做很好的产品。那里有编辑参与——尤其非常 product-minded 的编辑——带来他们最好的专长，和你在数据研究等洞察里找的正常信号结合。当你确保理解消费者问题、找到最好的创意解决方案时。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool.
turns.zh: 酷。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: It is really cool. It's one of the, I think, most gratifying parts of working at a news organization like the Times. But if you work on a different mission, like a monetization mission, we have two really big ones. One is subscriber growth, the other one that's also really important is digital advertising. They build centralized commercial products that we can then scale across all of the products in our bundle. The subscriber growth team, for instance, they look at making sure that we have really great account ID management for subscribers. If you're buying a subscription through games or through news. Or, if you're on the digital advertising team, you're trying to make sure that we have a first party data program that's really privacy safe, that works as well in cooking as it does in the news space.
turns.zh: 真的很酷。是在纽约时报这种新闻机构工作最 gratifying 的部分之一。但如果你在不同使命，比如变现使命，我们有两个大的。一是订阅者增长，另一个也重要的是数字广告。他们建可以跨 bundle 所有产品扩展的集中式商业产品。比如订阅者增长团队，他们看确保我们有很好的订阅者账户 ID 管理——不管你从游戏还是新闻买订阅。或数字广告团队，你试图确保我们有隐私安全的第一方数据 program，在烹饪和新闻都一样好 work。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: Then, there's a totally different third bucket of mission that we have, which is all of our platform teams. This is everything from monetization platforms like our commerce engine, which is so important, because we're a subscription business, to data platforms where you might have our ML platform or experimentation tooling, to just basic infrastructure. Those are shared across the bundle, which just really helps make it so much easier, more efficient for really engineers to ship code and do their best work. A lot of this actually, I think, probably is pretty familiar to how you might organize at a tech company minus the editors.
turns.zh: 然后还有完全不同的第三桶使命：所有平台团队。从变现平台如我们的商务引擎——超重要因为我们是订阅业务——到数据平台如 ML 平台或实验工具，到基础设施。这些跨 bundle 共享，真的帮工程师更容易更高效地 ship 代码、做最好工作。这大部分大概和科技公司组织方式很像，除了编辑。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. On that info piece, that reminds me of something I definitely wanted to talk about, which is something New York Times is really known for is the visualizations and these immersive stories that you all put out. I'm so curious just how that gets done. I feel like if I was on a product team at a regular, like a big tech FAANG company, I'd be like, "Shit, all these ad hoc things I got to do for all these stories, such a pain in the butt." That's so important to the New York Times and the online experience. I'm curious just like what is it like to build these things, say the election widgets, and all of that stuff?
turns.zh: 太好了。关于编辑那块让我想到一个我一定要聊的：纽约时报真的很出名的是可视化和沉浸式故事。我超好奇那怎么做的。我觉得如果我在常规大科技公司 FAANG 做产品团队，我会想「天哪，这些故事要做的 ad hoc 东西太多，太麻烦了」。但那对纽约时报和在线体验太重要。我好奇建那些东西是什么样的，比如选举 widget 那些？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Then, I don't know, I was just reading a story about climate change and it's this really beautiful immersive story of just what is happening with the world. There's a bunch of questions there, but I guess roughly just how does that get done, something like that?
turns.zh: 然后我刚在读一篇气候变化报道，就是这种很美的沉浸式故事。有一堆问题，但大概就是那种怎么做的？

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: Well, first, thanks for saying that. I really appreciate it. I do think there's something really special about some of the ways that we marry the journalism and the presentation. I want to start just by giving credit where credit's due, which is I think some of the most interesting and inventive and compelling formats, they actually do start off as one-off experiments that are spun up in the newsroom by embedded teams that we have within graphics, visual journalism, interactive news teams. This is where we have editors, journalists, engineers, data scientists, designers, literally all hunkered down together focusing on how to make one story come to life in the best possible way.
turns.zh: 首先谢谢你说。我很 appreciate。我确实觉得我们一些把新闻和呈现结合的方式很特别。我想先归功于该归功的人：一些最有趣、最有创意、最 compelling 的格式，其实是一一次性实验开始的，由我们嵌入在 graphics、视觉新闻、互动新闻团队里的团队在新闻编辑部发起。那里编辑、记者、工程师、数据科学家、设计师真的聚在一起聚焦怎么把一个故事以最好方式呈现。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Who has the idea usually? Is it like the journalists working on that, they're like, "Hey, I think we should make something really great."
turns.zh: 通常谁有 idea？是记者做的时候想「嘿，我们应该做点很棒的」？

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: Exactly. Yeah, one of the things ... We have a newsroom of over 2000 people. You basically have people who've been experts on certain beats like climate, for instance, for decades. They have the nugget of the idea. They start to do reporting and then they really pull in others from visuals, from interactive just to say, "How can I really make sure that I can tell this story with as much impact and weight as possible?" That's where the magic starts to happen, when you pull in all of those other skill sets together to help dream up how that story might be told.
turns.zh: 对。我们新闻编辑部有 2000 多人。你有在某些条线如气候做了几十年的专家。他们有 idea 的种子。开始报道，然后从视觉、互动拉人进来说「怎么确保我能以最大影响和分量讲这个故事？」那就是魔法开始发生的地方，当你拉进所有那些其他技能一起梦想故事怎么讲。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: They're like, "Alex, we need one of these for our story. Can you get us on the list?" How does that process go?
turns.zh: 他们像「Alex，我们的故事需要这种。你能把我们排上吗？」那个流程怎么走？

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: No, no, no. These are teams that are really autonomous in the newsroom. For one-off, truly special features, I'll give you an example of one that I found to be particularly powerful. I don't know if you read Jodi Kantor, who is one of our ... a really incredible investigative reporter. You might know for some of her work that she did around MeToo and Harvey Weinstein, in that investigation.
turns.zh: 不不不。这些是新闻编辑部里相当自主的团队。对于一次性的、真正特别的特稿，给你个我觉得特别有力的例子。不知道你读过 Jodi Kantor——我们一位非常 incredible 的调查记者。你可能知道她做的 MeToo 和 Harvey Weinstein 那个调查。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: She recently did a piece on how employers are tracking and monitoring remote workers with tools like productivity scores. The story itself was designed to show a person's own productivity score in the moment as they read the article.
turns.zh: 她最近做了一篇关于雇主怎么用生产力分数等工具追踪和监控远程员工的报道。故事本身设计成在你读文章时实时展示一个人自己的生产力分数。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, shit.
turns.zh: 天哪。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: It was super visceral, really creepy in the most effective way. In my mind, that's the type of magical experience that only happens when you actually have dedicated designers, engineers, and others who can really sit down with a reporter to say, "Let's figure out how to shape that story in the most magical way." The speed of news is so fast that you don't have time to mess with roadmaps. We really have teams who are freed up from some of the normal processes around that, so they can really just focus on storytelling for really big stories and pieces. But on top of that, what we do have is a storytelling product team. What they do is they really take notice of things that are starting to work in more of the experimental phase, some of these one-offs.
turns.zh: 非常直观，在最美妙的意义上很 creepy。对我来说，那是只有当你真的有 dedicated 设计师、工程师和其他人能坐下来和记者说「我们来 figure out 怎么以最神奇的方式塑造这个故事」才会发生的魔法体验。新闻速度太快，你没时间弄 roadmap。我们真的有团队从那些正常流程中解放出来，这样他们能专注为大故事讲故事。但除此之外，我们有个讲故事产品团队。他们注意在实验阶段开始 work 的一次性东西。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: Then, they work closely with editors to test and find product market fit for new formats that can actually scale across many parts of the report, so that over time when you open the app, the app is more accessible, more engaging, because we still have the traditional story based article, but we're also shifting more of the distribution of stories into video, into visuals, into live. If you even look at live, we've broken out of the tyranny of the article in many ways, where you have live reporter updates that are the size of length of tweets. People filing from the ground in Ukraine, trying to give you a sense of what's happening in a very immediate and real way.
turns.zh: 然后他们和编辑紧密合作，测试和找到可以扩展到报道多个部分的新格式的产品市场契合。这样随着时间你打开 app，app 更易用、更参与，因为我们仍有传统基于文章的故事，但我们也在把更多故事分发转成视频、视觉、live。即使看 live，我们已经从文章的暴政里突破了——有 live 记者更新，推文长度。人在乌克兰现场发稿，试图以非常即时真实的方式给你感觉发生了什么。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: That's where we do have teams, product teams who have to think in two modes. First, they have to be able to think in the moment with editors, where you might not always have all the right data at your fingertips and you just have to make a call, like, "What is the best experience to tell this story in a really truthful, accurate, accessible way?" Then, the other mode is when they're not shipping at the speed of news, they're trying to build end to end systems so that we're building the tooling to actually create the stories at the same time as the consumer experience, which is a totally different mode of system level thinking.
turns.zh: 那里我们确实有产品团队要在两种模式思考。首先，他们要能和编辑在当下思考，你可能不总有所有数据在手边就得做判断，如「以真实、准确、易用的方式讲这个故事的最佳体验是什么？」然后另一种模式是当他们不以新闻速度 ship 时，他们在试图建端到端系统，这样我们在建工具来创造故事的同时也在建消费者体验，这是完全不同的系统级思考模式。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: It's a very cool space. That product team is, they're pulling off some pretty incredible work because they can operate in those two modes. It's like, in the moment, in the moment of the story, but also trying to build the systems that allow you to reshape the composition of storytelling formats that we have across our products over time.
turns.zh: 是非常酷的空间。那个产品团队在做一些相当 incredible 的工作，因为他们能在那两种模式运作。当下、故事时刻，但也在试图建让你随时间重塑我们产品讲故事格式组合的系统。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is super cool. What percentage of these fancy stories are using that platform and building on something that already exists versus a one-off experiment would you say roughly?
turns.zh: 那超酷。这些花哨故事里大概多少百分比用那个平台、在已有东西上建 vs 一次性实验？

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: The majority are on our platforms hands down. Yeah. Yeah.
turns.zh: 大部分在我们的平台上，毫无疑问。对。对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. That makes sense. Then, just so I understand, so you said Jodi was the journalist?
turns.zh: 好，有道理。然后确认一下，你说 Jodi 是记者？

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You mentioned. Does she has a product team dedicated to her work?
turns.zh: 你提到。她有 dedicated 产品团队吗？

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: No, what we have is we have a centralized interactive news team, graphics team, data journalism team. Those editors partner with different journalists when they have really big stories to help bring their story to life.
turns.zh: 不，我们有集中式的互动新闻团队、graphics 团队、数据新闻团队。那些编辑和不同记者合作当他们有真正大故事时帮他们把故事呈现出来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I see. Do they have to come to this team and be like, "Hey, I'd love your time." How does that prioritization ... Because I imagine a lot of journalists are coming to them like, "Hey, my story is going to be awesome. We need you."
turns.zh: 懂了。他们要来找这个团队说「嘿，我想用你们时间」？那个优先级……因为我想象很多记者来找他们说「嘿，我的故事会很棒，我们需要你」。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: You know what? To be totally honest, I'm not involved. Somehow it works.
turns.zh: 你知道吗？完全说实话，我不参与。它就是 work 了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a great leadership sign. It just works and you set it up and it's working, so that's great.
turns.zh: 那是好的领导力信号。它就是 work 了，你搭好了、它在运转，太好了。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: Well, and the newsroom has set it up and something that is just, again, very interesting about the way that we are set up is that we have our newsroom and then we have our business side. The business side is where you have all of the product teams and there is intense collaboration between the two, but they do have different leadership structures because that's how we maintain the independence of our coverage. Our product teams sit within the newsroom if they're focused on storytelling, live, anything related to the coverage.
turns.zh: 而且新闻编辑部搭好了。关于我们怎么搭有一个很有意思的点：我们有新闻编辑部，然后有商业这边。商业这边是所有产品团队所在。两者之间有 intense 协作，但它们有不同的领导结构，因为这是我们保持报道独立性的方式。我们的产品团队如果聚焦于讲故事、live、任何与报道相关的，就坐在新闻编辑部里。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: The only distinction really that I think I'm trying to make is that product teams really help stories find their widest audience and be as engaging and as impactful as can be. But product teams don't have any influence over the selection of the stories. That is what the newsroom retains as editorial.
turns.zh: 我试图做的唯一区分是：产品团队帮故事找到最广受众、最有参与感、最有影响力。但产品团队对故事的选择没有任何影响。那是新闻编辑部保留的编辑独立。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. You mentioned Wordle and you all acquired Wordle recently. I'm just curious what that was all like. I imagine it's still being integrated. Were you involved in the exploration and purchase process and what went on there?
turns.zh: 好。你提到 Wordle，你们最近收购了 Wordle。我好奇那是怎么回事。我猜它还在整合中。你参与了探索和收购过程吗？发生了什么？

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: Wordle has been such a fun ride. Maybe I'll first just bring you behind the scenes on how the deal came to be, and then we can talk a little bit more about what the integration process has been like.
turns.zh: Wordle 是一段很好玩的旅程。也许我先带你看看 deal 怎么来的，然后我们再聊整合过程。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, sounds great.
turns.zh: 好，听起来很好。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: I first heard about Wordle in early January because a New York Times reporter, Daniel Victor, actually wrote a piece about Josh Wardle, who's a software engineer in Brooklyn, and how he had created the game. It really is this gesture of love for his partner, and I certainly wasn't the only person to read through that column. Everyone inside the New York Times perked up. I remember reaching out to Jonathan Knight, who's the general manager of games, he's on my team. He had already taken notice well before the piece was published, and he had already reached out to Josh to see if he would be interested in having games join our portfolio.
turns.zh: 我一月最早听说 Wordle，因为纽约时报记者 Daniel Victor 写了一篇关于 Josh Wardle 的报道，他是布鲁克林的软件工程师，怎么创造的这个游戏。那真的是他给伴侣的爱意表达，我当然不是唯一读到那篇专栏的人。纽约时报内部所有人都注意到了。我记得联系 Jonathan Knight，游戏总经理，我团队的人。他在那篇出来之前就注意到了，已经联系 Josh 看他是否有兴趣让游戏加入我们的组合。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: We just all loved Wordle immediately because if you've played it, it shares a lot of the DNA of other really successful word games that we have at the New York Times, like Spelling Bee or the Crossword Mini. If anything, Josh was really forthright that he created it because he was inspired by those games. Then, in the context of just our subscription strategy, games is such an important category for us. We really see games and demand for games as this, basically, it's a counterpoint to the news. It gives people a chance to actually take a break. It's fun. It doesn't feel like empty calories. It's really time well spent.
turns.zh: 我们都立刻爱上 Wordle，因为如果你玩过，它和我们其他成功字游如 Spelling Bee 或 Crossword Mini 共享很多 DNA。Josh 也非常坦率说他创造它是受那些游戏启发。在我们的订阅策略里，游戏是重要类别。我们真的把游戏和游戏需求看作新闻的反面。它让人喘口气。有趣。不是空热量。是花得值的时间。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: We were just thinking of Wordle as such a wonderful addition to our games franchise to really give people more reasons to feel like they had a relationship with the New York Times every day. The whole thesis of the acquisition just made so much sense. Our team just very quickly engaged with Josh and the acquisition talks were incredibly fast. The whole thing took place in a matter of weeks, which is way faster than any other acquisition I've been a part of. It was a very amicable process. We were just super delighted to bring Wordle on board, but it happened in record speed.
turns.zh: 我们觉得 Wordle 是游戏品牌的绝佳补充，让人每天更有理由觉得和纽约时报有关系。收购的整个 thesis 非常合理。我们团队很快和 Josh 接触，收购谈判极快。整个事情几周内完成，比我参与过的任何收购都快。非常友好。我们很高兴把 Wordle 带上船，但它的速度是破纪录的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well, yeah, it felt fast from the outside too. It became a huge deal. Then, "Okay, New York Times buys them." Yeah, it's impressive. You said you acquired Athletic. How often are you acquiring companies?
turns.zh: 嗯，对，从外面看也觉得快。它成了大 deal。然后「好，纽约时报买了他们。」厉害。你说你们收购了 The Athletic。你们多久收购一次公司？

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: We also acquired The Athletic, and that was back in around the same time. I think for now we feel like we actually ... we have all of the major categories to make the essential subscription work. For us to get to 15 million subscribers we really feel like news, sports, games, cooking, audio and shopping, those are the categories, and we just have to make them the best possible versions of themselves, those products, so that we can really provide just tremendous value every day to people. That doesn't mean that we won't make some other acquisitions. The next Wordle would absolutely love to hear about it.
turns.zh: 我们也收购了 The Athletic，差不多同期。我觉得现在我们真的有了让必备订阅 work 的所有主要类别。要达 1500 万订阅者我们真的觉得新闻、体育、游戏、烹饪、音频和购物就是那些类别，我们只需把它们做成最好版本，这样每天给人巨大价值。这不意味着我们不会再做别的收购。下一个 Wordle 我们绝对想听。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: But I do think there's also a real lesson for a lot of companies, not only about when you acquire what's the opportunity, but also are you ready to actually integrate an acquisition? We learned a lot just around Wordle in terms of what that process is like. I just want to say I'm really proud of how thoughtful and considerate our games team was about the integration process, because Wordle players feel such connection to the game. We really wanted to make sure not to interfere with the core magic of the experience. If you are an eight-year old kid or an 88-year old adult, there's real resonance with Wordle and people just have such a connection to it. We really wanted to make sure we didn't mess it up. Do you want to go a little bit deeper, just almost what that looks like?
turns.zh: 但我觉得对很多公司也有个真实教训：不只关于收购时机会是什么，还有你 ready 真正整合收购吗？我们在 Wordle 上学了很多关于那个过程。我只想说我非常自豪游戏团队在整合过程中多么周到体贴，因为 Wordle 玩家对游戏有那么强连接。我们真的想确保不干扰体验的核心魔法。不管你是 8 岁小孩还是 88 岁老人，Wordle 真的 resonant，人有那么强连接。我们真的想确保不搞砸。你想再深一点说吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, absolutely.
turns.zh: 对，绝对。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: Because we definitely learned a lot. When we acquired Wordle, it was a simple web game with no backend. That meant that people's stats and streaks, which was that was the value in terms of social currency that people were sharing after playing, those stats and streaks were stored in local browsers. It was really important for us to make sure that the game board experience in the core loop of the game remained unchanged. But we also found that because everything was stored locally and people care so much about their stats and streaks, if they got a new iPhone, if they switched browsers, all of a sudden they lost all of that history that they had with the game.
turns.zh: 因为我们确实学了很多。我们收购 Wordle 时，它是个简单 web 游戏，没有后端。意味着人的统计和连胜——那是玩后分享的社交货币——存在本地浏览器里。确保游戏板体验和核心循环不变很重要。但我们也发现因为一切存在本地、人在乎统计和连胜，换了 iPhone、换了浏览器，突然所有历史都没了。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: What we decided to do was undertake a project to connect Wordle to a New York Times account, which was free, because Wordle is a free game, just so that it knows who you are and so that your stats and streaks can be protected. Then, we could also bring Wordle to more surfaces because we wanted ... if you go to the homepage of the news app or if you go to the games app, we wanted to make it easier to find because people would come for Spelling Bee or Crosswords and they also wanted their Wordle. It was a pretty big effort to rewrite Wordle in our tech stack, give people the ability to store their stats and streaks, bring games to all of our major surfaces.
turns.zh: 我们决定做的是把 Wordle 连接到纽约时报账号——免费，因为 Wordle 是免费游戏——这样它知道你是谁、统计和连胜受保护。然后我们也能把 Wordle 带到更多面，因为我们想……如果你去新闻 app 首页或游戏 app，我们想让它更容易找到，因为人来玩 Spelling Bee 或 Crossword 也想玩 Wordle。在我们的技术栈里重写 Wordle、让人能存统计和连胜、把游戏带到所有主要面，是挺大的工程。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: We just tried to do it in a thoughtful way, where we didn't break anything. The experience was hopefully seamless, and that the only thing you would notice that's changed is that the New York Times knows enough about who you are so that your stats carry over and you can play anywhere. But that doesn't mean that there aren't some surprises along the way, especially when you're doing backend work. We had this pretty crazy moment a couple months ago, right when the Supreme Court's draft ruling on Roe v. Wade leaked. An engineer on the games team happened to notice that the Wordle solution the next day was fetus. Which is just an extraordinarily bad coincidence, because the word had been loaded into the game by the game founder months beforehand.
turns.zh: 我们试图以周到方式做，不破坏任何东西。体验希望无缝，你唯一注意到的变化是纽约时报知道你是谁以便统计延续、你可以在任何地方玩。但这不意味着过程中没有意外，尤其做后端工作时。我们几个月前有个相当疯狂的时刻，就在最高法院罗诉韦德案草案裁决泄露时。游戏团队一个工程师碰巧注意到第二天 Wordle 答案是 fetus。这是个极其糟糕的巧合，因为那个词是游戏创始人几个月前就加载进去的。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: It was so important for us that we didn't have ... this lovely diversion from the news feel almost like it was commentary on a very contentious story that was happening. I don't know if you caught wind of that, but you'd think that you could easily change the word on the backend, but because we were midstream on the migration process and some users were on the original Wordle game, others had migrated to the new version. It meant that we actually couldn't change the word on the backend for everyone, only for some people. This was a moment where we just had to come out and really tell the world, "We're mid integration. We're really not trying to communicate more than Wordle being a fun diversion from the news. Here's what happened, and why."
turns.zh: 我们非常重要的是不要让这个可爱的新闻消遣感觉像在对一个非常敏感的故事做评论。不知道你听说了没，但你会想你可以轻松在后端改词，但因为我们正在迁移中、有些用户在原版 Wordle、有些已迁到新版本，意味着我们其实没法为所有人改后端的词，只能为部分人。这是个我们不得不出来告诉世界的时刻：「我们正在整合中。我们真的没想表达 Wordle 不只是新闻的有趣消遣之外的东西。这是发生了什么以及为什么。」

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: Everyone understood. This is where coming out being really transparent about the facts and in some cases just exposing more about the product development process really helps demystify some of the rumors that people might otherwise think. It was one of those like, "Oh, man, I couldn't have imagined that that type of terrible coincidence would happen." But you just have to be prepared for everything, even when you're integrating what should just be a fun game.
turns.zh: 大家都理解了。这就是出来对事实非常透明、有时暴露更多产品开发过程真的帮澄清人可能有的谣言。那是那种「天哪我想不到那种糟糕巧合会发生」的时刻。但你就是得为一切做好准备，即使你只是在整合一个应该只是好玩的游戏。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Imagine, no matter what you tell people, some folks are just not going to believe a very simple explanation of what was going on.
turns.zh: 想象，不管你怎么说，有些人就是不信一个简单的解释。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: It's true. All you can do is be as honest and transparent. What I will say is a lot of people still think we try to make Wordle harder, we don't, I promise. It's not a thing.
turns.zh: 对。你只能尽量诚实透明。我要说的是很多人仍觉得我们试图让 Wordle 更难，我们没有，我保证。不是那么回事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, it's not like the crossword puzzle where it gets harder every day of the week.
turns.zh: 对，它不是那种每天变难的 crossword。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: No, no. It's not, it's not.
turns.zh: 不不。不是不是。

turns.zh: 去 vanta.com/lenny。V-A-N-T-A.com/lenny 了解更多并领折扣。今天就开始。还有没有别的故事反映在纽约时报做产品 leader 多有趣/疯狂？

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: If we could of go back to when I started at the New York Times, because I started in late 2019, it was just right before the pandemic. It was pretty wild to come back to the company and to get shifted into this moment of needing to build products that really were trying to help people through the moment. At a time when our journalists were covering the story and all of New York Times' employees were trying to live through it. It was COVID 24/7 in terms of work and life. For me, I remember in the earliest days when we were first really reporting on COVID and learning about it, we had reporters on the ground in Wuhan even before we knew how COVID was transmitted.
turns.zh: 回到我开始纽约时报时，2019 年底，就在疫情前。回来就进入这个需要做产品帮人度过时刻的时刻，挺疯狂的。当时我们的记者在报道这个故事、所有纽约时报员工在试图熬过它。工作生活都是 COVID 24/7。对我来说，我记得最早我们刚开始报道 COVID、了解它时，我们有记者在武汉现场，甚至在我们知道 COVID 怎么传播之前。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: Then, when the world shut down, for the Times, we went fully remote in March, 2020, and I remember the day so well because it was the beginning of spring break, of course, all plans were canceled. My kids, I had no idea what to do with them. My husband and I panic packed, put them in a car, drove to go see some friends in Vermont, and we decided we were going to do a kid daycare pool share just to figure out how to keep working with someone overseeing the kids. We got there late at night and I literally just went into a laundry closet and I didn't emerge for two weeks because my Slack was blowing up about all of the work that we needed to do to make our products as useful as possible.
turns.zh: 然后世界停摆。对纽约时报来说我们 2020 年 3 月完全远程。我记得那天那么清楚，因为是春假开始、当然所有计划取消。我孩子我不知道怎么办。我丈夫和我慌忙打包、放车上、开去看佛蒙特的朋友，我们决定搞个孩子 daycare 共享 pool 来 figure out 怎么继续工作有人看孩子。我们深夜到，我 literally 进了一个洗衣间、两周没出来，因为 Slack 被所有要让产品尽可能有用的工作轰炸。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: The kids were being crazy and we just had to get to work. What was really stunning about this moment in time was that as people were getting sick and we were reporting about all of the trends that we were seeing, we saw that other institutions, especially the government, were not actually stepping up to help people understand the basic facts about what was happening. This is a product leader, it's a real wartime moment where you just need to blow up roadmaps, share context with everyone and say, "Okay, everyone, we have a totally different mandate than what we did a couple weeks ago." Given the needs in the world and the mission of the New York Times and our purpose, which is to help people access information to make informed decision about their lives, we're going to do a whole bunch of these things.
turns.zh: 孩子们在发疯，我们就是得工作。那个时刻最 stunning 的是随着人在生病、我们在报道趋势，我们看到其他机构尤其政府没有真的站出来帮人理解基本事实。作为产品 leader，这是真正的战时时刻，你就是要炸掉 roadmap、和所有人共享上下文说「好，大家，我们的 mandate 和几周前完全不同。」鉴于世界需求和纽约时报的使命和目的——帮人获取信息做明智决策——我们要做一大堆这些事。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: We're going to build a comprehensive public data set of COVID cases. Nobody else is doing it. We really just started scraping and pulling this together, and what was a single spreadsheet at the time. We pulled a bunch of engineers from other teams to go help build out that database. We launched entirely new formats and data tools to make our journalism a lot more easier to follow. Things like tools to be able to look up infection rates and eventually vaccination rates down at your local zip code level. We made our most important COVID coverage free to everybody. It was really important that if it was something related to public safety, we didn't put it behind a paywall.
turns.zh: 我们要建一个全面的 COVID 病例公共数据集。没别人在做。我们真的开始爬取和拼凑，当时就是一张电子表格。我们从别的团队拉一批工程师去帮建那个数据库。我们上线全新的格式和数据工具让新闻更易跟进。比如能查到你的 zip code 级别感染率、后来疫苗接种率的工具。我们让最重要的 COVID 报道对所有人免费。如果和公共安全相关，不放在付费墙后很重要。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: Our mission is to do better than that. We really made sure that we had that information available to everyone. We also just found that for journalists who hadn't actually been in Wuhan, they just needed tips to an internal safety guidance for reporting, and so we made that publicly available. It was just one of those really interesting moments where everything felt so crazy in this moment of crisis. But building purposeful products that made a really difficult moment feel not only possible but promising, was one of the most unifying moments, I would say, for our teams.
turns.zh: 我们的使命是做得更好。我们确保那个信息对所有人可用。我们还发现没去过武汉的记者需要内部安全报道指南的 tips，于是我们把它公开了。那是个相当有趣的时刻，一切感觉那么疯狂。但做有目的的产品让一个艰难时刻感觉不仅可能而且有希望，是对我们团队最统一的时刻之一。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: Because even though people were working so hard and balancing work life and personal life, no one doubted for a second that the work they were doing was of greater good for the world. There's real privilege in being able to spend your time doing those things. But it's one of the biggest news stories of our lifetime and to be at the forefront of that, I think for all of us, was a pretty incredible and humbling experience.
turns.zh: 因为虽然大家工作那么努力、在工作生活和个人生活间平衡，没人一秒怀疑他们做的是对世界更大的善。能花时间做那些事是真正的特权。那是我们这代人最大的新闻故事之一，走在前沿对所有人来说都是非常 incredible 和谦卑的经历。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. People talk about having impact and driving impact and it's usually like, move this metric some percentage, but that is some incredible impact. Helping people avoid COVID, avoid dying, keeping their families safe. It's got to be some of the most fulfilling work that you and your team has done and ideally it wouldn't have happened, but it was also probably incredibly fulfilling.
turns.zh: 哇。大家说有影响、驱动影响，通常是把这个指标移动百分之几，但那是难以置信的影响。帮人避免 COVID、避免死亡、保护家人安全。这一定是你和团队做过的最有成就感的工作之一，理想情况它不会发生，但也可能极其有成就感。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: Thank you for saying that. One of the most validating tricks that we did look at was we realized that at the height of the pandemic, when there was just so much confusion about literally what to do, how to live each day in March, 2020, we saw that half of the country came to the New York Times. There is something again that is just so powerful about very straightforward data journalism, deep reporting, service guidance on how to make a mask if you don't have one. Just like all of these basics. Just seeing the whole organization pivot from their normal job into this mode and was pretty incredible, and the world responded, which was really validating too.
turns.zh: 谢谢你这么说。我们看的最 validating 的一件事是：在疫情高峰、大家对每天该怎么做那么困惑时，2020 年 3 月，我们看到半个国家的人都来了纽约时报。非常直接的数据新闻、深度报道、服务指导如怎么做口罩这些基础的东西，就是有那种力量。看到整个组织从正常工作转到这个模式相当 incredible，世界也回应了，那很 validating。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I imagine there's also a bit of burnout that happens working, where it goes on and on and on. You're like, "Oh, my God, when is this going to slow down?" How do you help people avoid burnout? How do you catch burnout as a leader on a product team?
turns.zh: 我想象也有职业倦怠，一直工作一直工作。你像「天哪什么时候会慢下来？」你怎么帮人避免倦怠？作为产品 leader 你怎么发现倦怠？

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: This is one of the most honestly, hard and important topics that I think we're always still grappling with. As a company, we really did try to lead originally with giving people more time off, more support, like financial support and other assistance with daycare, health benefits, all of the basics. I think now what we're really trying to do beyond that is be so much more focused on the things that we need to do and all of the things that we're really happy to stop doing. Because part of, I think, context switching is one of the things that is really, really difficult. It's hard to context switch in your job.
turns.zh: 这是我老实说觉得我们一直在挣扎的最难最重要的话题之一。作为公司我们真的最初试图带头给更多休假、更多支持如 daycare 财务支持、健康福利等基础。我觉得现在我们在那之外更聚焦于我们必须做的事和很乐意停做的事。因为上下文切换是非常困难的事之一。在工作里上下文切换就难。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: It's really hard to context switch across your job and your life. There are a lot of things that we as a company can't necessarily control in people's lives, but within the job, the places where we can be so much more focused and thoughtful about the small number of important things that we must do at a given point in time, that's really the place where we're really trying to come in and be as empathetic and as honest about what we need to do and what we don't need to do. A lot of it really comes down to, I think, making hard calls. We're not always perfect at it. I'm sure that there are things that we could be more diligent about.
turns.zh: 跨工作和生活切换更难。我们作为公司在人的生活里有很多没法控制的事，但在工作里，我们能更聚焦和周到地对待那一小撮我们必须在给定时刻做的重要事情的地方，就是我们试图进来、对要做什么和不要做什么尽可能 empathetic 和诚实的地方。很多真的归结于做难判断。我们不是总完美。肯定有我们可以更勤奋的地方。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: But I would say over on balance, we've seen a lot of people stay at the company because they're figuring out they work remotely, maybe they come back to the office. They're figuring out how to live their life in a very different way from a couple of years ago. We're really here to try to meet them and make that as possible as possible. We need incredible people across a bunch of different skill sets, a bunch of different backgrounds. The only way to do that is to really be very flexible and accommodating in terms of trying to meet people where they are in their lives, but it's tricky.
turns.zh: 但总体来说我们看到很多人留在公司，因为他们在 figure out 远程工作、也许回办公室。他们在 figure out 怎么以非常不同于几年前的方式生活。我们真的在试图 meet 他们、让那尽可能可能。我们需要各种技能、各种背景的 incredible 的人。唯一办法就是非常灵活和 accommodating，试图在他们的生活里 meet 他们，但很 tricky。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: There is no perfect answer for this, but we're really trying because the success of the company only works when we have people who feel valued and they can do their best work and live really rich lives on top of that. I think we're all still figuring out what that looks like now that we're starting to come out of the official pandemic and really just learning how to live with COVID.
turns.zh: 没有完美答案，但我们真的在试，因为公司成功只有在人觉得被重视、能做最好工作、还能过丰富生活时才行。我觉得我们都还在 figure out 现在我们开始走出正式疫情、真的在学习怎么和 COVID 共处。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Right, absolutely. You mentioned that you're all remote now. Is that the policy going forward?
turns.zh: 对，完全同意。你说你们现在全远程。这是未来政策吗？

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: We actually just started going back into the office a couple of days per week, which is very encouraged. We're still finding our groove. We do have a good number of people though who are fully remote as well. It's more of an evolution in terms of trying to find the right balance of taking advantage of in-person work, because there are some moments where it really does make such a difference when you have people together working through hard problems in real life. That camaraderie, those relationships really, really do matter. Also, being realistic about the fact that there are a lot of people who would love to work at the New York Times, but might not be able to live in the New York City area.
turns.zh: 其实我们刚开始每周回办公室几天，非常鼓励。我们还在找节奏。但我们确实有不少完全远程的人。更多是个进化，试图找对平衡，利用线下工作因为有些时刻人在一起实时处理难问题真的有很大差别。那种同志情谊、关系真的很重要。也要现实地看到很多人想在纽约时报工作但可能没法住纽约地区。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: So, how do we make sure that we can be a remote friendly company for them too? Yeah, so we're very hybrid, we're still testing our way through it. But by and large, we're shipping so much tremendous work, which I think is a reflection of us being able to do the hybrid thing and just try to get better and better at it each day, each week.
turns.zh: 所以我们怎么确保对他们也是个远程友好公司？对，我们非常 hybrid，还在试。但总的来说我们 ship 了非常多出色的工作，这反映我们能做 hybrid 这件事并试着每天每周更好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, it's hard. As an outsider, I can't imagine a New York Times being all remote. It feels like that kind of company just, it's all happening in a building somewhere probably. I'm also a big fan of in-person, it feels like as a company, it feels like you have an advantage if you're working in-person generally.
turns.zh: 对，很难。作为局外人，我没法想象纽约时报全远程。感觉那种公司就是在一栋楼里发生。我也很喜欢线下，感觉公司如果线下工作会有优势。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: We certainly see that, and so the center of gravity is in New York and is in the office, but again, with a lot of flexibility for people's lives. We're really trying to figure out that balance.
turns.zh: 我们确实看到，重心在纽约、在办公室，但对人的生活有很多灵活。我们在 figure out 那个平衡。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just a couple more questions before we get to our very exciting lightning round. Where's the New York Times in the next five, 10 years as a product specifically different from other folks? Then, broadly, I don't know, if you have any insights or opinions on just what is the future of news, do share.
turns.zh: 闪电问答前还有几个问题。纽约时报作为产品未来 5 到 10 年和别的什么不同？然后宽泛地说，如果你对新闻的未来有洞察或看法，也分享。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: I think the New York Times is in a pretty unique spot compared to other news organizations right now. I have tremendous respect for other high quality organizations like The Journal and The Post and The FT and The Guardian. They're just doing such incredible work. But when I go back to what differentiates us, it's this idea of becoming an essential subscription that really helps people. It meets their most important news and life needs across all of the categories that we've been talking about, like news, games, audio, cooking, et cetera.
turns.zh: 我觉得纽约时报相比其他新闻机构现在位置相当独特。我非常尊重其他高质量机构如华尔街日报、华盛顿邮报、FT、Guardian。它们做得 incredible 的工作。但回到我们的差异化，是成为真正帮人的必备订阅，在新闻、游戏、音频、烹饪等我们聊的所有类别里 meet 他们最重要的新闻和生活需求。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: Up until, I would say, this year we were more of a news brand with a collection of adjacent lifestyle products, but with the acquisition of Wordle and the Athletic, along with just the continued growth of cooking and Wirecutter and some of our other offerings, I really do think that has transformed us into a brand capable of really being that essential subscription that helps every single day people with news and life needs in a way that doesn't just associate the New York Times with [inaudible 00:52:12] categories. Imagine that you open the New York Times app and you are starting with a great breaking news story. Then, you skip over to the latest coverage in China.
turns.zh: 直到今年我们更像一个有一系列相邻生活方式产品的新闻品牌，但有了 Wordle 和 The Athletic 的收购、加上烹饪和 Wirecutter 等的持续增长，我真觉得那让我们变成了一个有能力成为每天在新闻和生活需求上帮人的必备订阅的品牌，不只是把纽约时报和硬新闻类别关联。想象你打开纽约时报 app，从一个好的突发新闻故事开始。然后跳到中国最新报道。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: Then, you decide that you want to take a small break to play Spelling Bee, and then you want to plan a Korean dinner party with Eric Kim, who I don't know if you know has some of the best Korean recipes. He's amazing. Then, you're like, "Wow, I need a rice cooker to be able to make that recipe, so I need to go get the best recommendation from Wirecutter."
turns.zh: 然后你想歇一下玩 Spelling Bee，然后你想用 Eric Kim 的韩式晚宴食谱规划——不知道你知不知道他有最好的韩式食谱，他太棒了。然后你想「哇我需要电饭煲来做那个食谱，我得去 Wirecutter 找最好的推荐。」

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I just did exactly that, actually.
turns.zh: 我刚做了这个。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: Did you?
turns.zh: 是吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: Then, I would love to go watch the Britney Spears documentary, which is also part of the New York Times franchise, which is amazing. Or, I want to go listen to Kevin Roose and Casey Newton's Hard Fork podcast, which is wildly fun and just launched a couple weeks ago, if you haven't heard that. This is, I think, the future for us of being a connected family of products, where we can meet so many different needs that are first anchored in news, but then stretched into other facets of your lives. I don't really see other news organizations really operating at that scale and that ambition, and that's the future for us.
turns.zh: 然后我想去看 Britney Spears 纪录片，也是纽约时报品牌的，很棒。或我想听 Kevin Roose 和 Casey Newton 的 Hard Fork 播客，非常好玩，刚上线几周如果你还没听。这就是我们的未来——成为连接的产品家族，能 meet 这么多首先锚定在新闻、但延伸到生活其他方面的需求。我真没看到其他新闻机构在那种规模和雄心上运作。这是我们的未来。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: We really just think that the New York Times can mean so much more to so many more people. We're a journalism company, but we're building just tremendous software, and so the product ambitions are only getting bigger and bigger, and that's why I feel like I've got the luckiest job in the world right now.
turns.zh: 我们真的觉得纽约时报可以对更多人意味更多。我们是新闻公司，但我们在做 tremendous 的软件，所以产品雄心只会在变大。这就是为什么我觉得我有世界上最幸运的工作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is a compelling vision. I feel like you can build your own metaverse in the New York Times where you just spend all of your days inside the New York Times' suite of products.
turns.zh: 那是个 compelling 的愿景。我觉得你可以在纽约时报建自己的元宇宙，整天泡在纽约时报产品套件里。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: Can I say though, there is a big difference. I think that for us our software actually helps people with real world outcomes in a very different way. We basically help you get access to information, decide how you're going to go to the ballot box. We give you information to go cook. Actually, there's something that I think is even more of a connection to the physical world, and it is very different from what the Metaverse is doing, but that's where we feel like we can drive as much impact as possible.
turns.zh: 但我能说有个大区别。我觉得我们的软件其实帮人达到真实世界的结果，非常不同。我们帮你获取信息、决定怎么投票。给你信息去 cook。其实和物理世界有更深的连接，和元宇宙做的非常不同，但那正是我们觉得能驱动最大影响的地方。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You can have your own competing metaverse. Here's a quick Wirecutter suggest idea for you, while we're chatting. I feel like Wirecutter, I use it all the time, everything I buy is based on Wirecutter recommendations, but I feel like there's an opportunity for design oriented version of Wirecutter. I don't know if anyone's thinking about that.
turns.zh: 你可以有自己的竞争元宇宙。这里有个 Wirecutter 建议给你，我们聊着。我觉得 Wirecutter 我一直用，买什么基于 Wirecutter 推荐，但我觉得有机会做设计导向版 Wirecutter。不知道有没有人在想。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: Tell me more.
turns.zh: 多说说。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just Wirecutter's functional stuff. It's like, "Here's the best, I don't know, rice cooker." But like, what's the cutest but also the best? What's the cross section of looks good in my house and is the best. I'll be okay not the best best if it looks nicer, so a design lens to Wirecutter.
turns.zh: Wirecutter 是功能性的。「这是最好的电饭煲。」但什么最可爱又最好？好看和最好的交集是什么？我可以接受不是最好如果更好看，给 Wirecutter 加设计 lens。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: If it's Wirecutter meets high taste, basically. I like that. I like that. Okay.
turns.zh: Wirecutter 遇上高品味。我喜欢。我喜欢。好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think there's a market there.
turns.zh: 我觉得那里有市场。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: I'll definitely bring that back to the team. That's a good one.
turns.zh: 我一定带回去给团队。好主意。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There you go. Well, we've reached our very exciting lightning round where I'm just going to ask you, I have six questions, I'll get through them pretty quick. Whatever comes to mind, fire off. We'll go through it fast and fun. Sound good?
turns.zh: 看。我们到了非常精彩的闪电问答，我有六个问题，很快过。想到什么就答。我们快速有趣。好吗？

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: Great.
turns.zh: 好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. What are two or three books that you recommend most to other people?
turns.zh: 好。你最常推荐给人的两三本书？

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: I love Stripe Press, and so I think a lot of the books that they have are just such good references, like Elad Gill's High Growth Handbook, or Will Larson's An Elegant Puzzle. Then, some of the more topical ones like Revolt of the Public. I just find that they're evergreen in terms of their utility. Anyone can find value in them. I just loved the craft of the books themselves. They are amazing products in terms of the content and the form, so those are, in the product context and work context, those are hands down I would say the places where I go first.
turns.zh: 我喜欢 Stripe Press，他们出的很多书都是很好的参考，如 Elad Gill 的 High Growth Handbook、Will Larson 的 An Elegant Puzzle。还有更话题性的如 Revolt of the Public。我觉得它们在实用性上常青。任何人都能从中获得价值。我也爱那些书的 craft 本身。它们在内容和形式上都是 amazing 产品，所以在产品和工作语境下这是我首先去的地方。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: But I do think, and I know this is this humanities major in me, I also always try to balance books and my own reading time and recommendations with fiction. I just think it's actually like, sometimes some of the best ideas and inspiration come when you go one or two steps away from the core books that are related to your practice. Right now, I'm actually rereading Giovanni's Room by James Baldwin. It's just so beautiful and so lyrical and it gets at more components of the human soul that, I know it sounds crazy, but I find like those are little sparks of ideas that ultimately come back into making products, and particularly news products where they're so creative in the way that they tell stories.
turns.zh: 但我也确实——我知道这是我身上的人文学科特质——总在平衡书籍和自己的阅读时间与推荐，加小说。我觉得有时最好的 idea 和灵感来自你离和你实践相关的核心书籍一两步之外。现在我其实在重读 James Baldwin 的 Giovanni's Room。太美太抒情，触及人类灵魂更多面向，我知道听起来疯狂，但我觉得那些是 idea 的小火花，最终会回到做产品里，尤其新闻产品在讲故事方式上那么有创意。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: I always try to give people one pragmatic recommendation and then one slightly more field recommendation over in the world of fiction. If you haven't read Giovanni's Room, it is incredible and devastating, and I absolutely recommend it.
turns.zh: 我总试着给人一个务实推荐加一个更偏小说的推荐。如果你没读过 Giovanni's Room，它 incredible 且毁灭性，我绝对推荐。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. I feel like I just keep buying books after doing these podcasts. I have so many books I got to read. I'm also feeling like the combination of books you recommended is exactly what I would imagine someone leading product at New York Times would recommend, something product tactical and then just a beautiful piece of fiction.
turns.zh: 哇。我觉得做完这些播客后我一直在买书。我有好多书要读。我也觉得你推荐的书的组合正是我想象中领导纽约时报产品的人会推荐的——产品战术加美丽小说。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: I'm the cliché. I love it.
turns.zh: 我是 cliché。我爱。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Great. No, no, no. I wouldn't put it that way. Okay. What's a favorite other podcast that you like to listen to? You mentioned one already, is that the one?
turns.zh: 好。不不不。我不会那么说。好。你最喜欢听的其他播客？你已经提了一个，是那个吗？

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: Everyone should listen to Hard Fork. It's great. But I just think The Daily continues to be, and again, I know it sounds self-serving, but being able to just listen to Michael Barbaro and Sabrina Tavernise once a day, just bring in journalists to talk and unpack a meaningful story, it's so visceral. I just find it to be one of the daily miracles that the New York Times is able to produce.
turns.zh: 大家都该听 Hard Fork。很棒。但我觉得 The Daily 仍然是——我知道听起来自利——但每天能听 Michael Barbaro 和 Sabrina Tavernise 带记者来 unpack 一个有意义的故事，太直观。我觉得那是纽约时报能产出的每日奇迹之一。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, that's wild. I can't imagine a daily thing like that doing that. Impressive. What's a recent favorite movie or TV show that you've seen that you've really enjoyed?
turns.zh: 对，不可思议。我没法想象每天做那种。厉害。最近最喜欢的电影或剧集？

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: I am pretty old school. I am actually rewatching The Wire for the third time.
turns.zh: 我比较老派。我其实在第三次重看 The Wire。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. That's a lot of time commitment.
turns.zh: 哇。那时间投入不少。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: It is. I have very little time, but every five years my husband and I, we just can't get over the characters, the storylines. It's just one of the best made series for television ever. It's a work of art, and so I am that person, that is another cliché, who is rewatching The Wire right now.
turns.zh: 是。我时间很少，但每五年我丈夫和我就是放不下那些角色、故事线。它是电视史上最好的剧集之一。是艺术品。所以我就是那个人，又一个 cliché，在重看 The Wire。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's your favorite season?
turns.zh: 你最喜欢哪季？

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: I would probably say it's season three, but when Stringer Bell passes away, it's the culmination of just so much. I probably shouldn't say that for anyone who hasn't seen The Wire. Oh, that's like the worst thing ever.
turns.zh: 我大概说第三季，但 Stringer Bell 去世时，是太多东西的 culmination。我大概不该对没看过 The Wire 的人说。哦那是最糟的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Spoiler alert in reverse.
turns.zh: 反向剧透警告。

turns.en: Spoiler alert. I'm so sorry.
