turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: But that's not the character name, that's the actor, right?
turns.zh: 但那不是角色名，是演员吧？

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: No, no, I really just totally spoiled that.
turns.zh: 不不，我真的 totally 剧透了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, that's cool. If you haven't seen it at this point, it's over, your loss.
turns.zh: 好，没事。如果你到现在没看过，就这样了，你的损失。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: Oh, boy. How awful. That's like a cardinals sin. But I do think season four, when it starts to get into the school system is also just, the actors are incredible. It's some of the best acting that I think has existed over the last couple of decades. Again, if you haven't seen it, please do yourself a favor and watch it. It's worth every episode.
turns.zh: 天哪。多糟。那是个 cardinal 罪。但第四季开始进入学校系统时也——演员太棒了。是过去几十年最好的演技之一。如果你没看过，请帮自己一个忙看看。每一集都值得。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Would you agree season two is the worst?
turns.zh: 你同意第二季最差吗？

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: I thought that until I re-watched it.
turns.zh: 我之前那么想直到重看。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Interesting.
turns.zh: 有意思。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: I actually came around and it's not at the top of my list, but there's more to it than I think I originally gave it credit for.
turns.zh: 我其实改观了，不在列表顶部，但比我最初给的有更多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. I like this. Okay, great. What are four to five SaaS products that you or company uses most that you find really useful?
turns.zh: 哇。我喜欢。好。你们公司最常用的四五个 SaaS 产品？

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: Probably pretty classic, we use G-Suite, Slack, Figma, Mode, GitHub. Those are the ones that I think just get hands down the most amount of usage across our teams.
turns.zh: 大概很经典：G-Suite、Slack、Figma、Mode、GitHub。那些是跨团队使用最多的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The fourth one was Mode?
turns.zh: 第四个是 Mode？

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there any interesting new recent one that's like top of mind while we're on this topic?
turns.zh: 有有趣的、新的、最近的吗？

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: Not really. No.
turns.zh: 不太有。不。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, great. The winners keep winning, huh? These products?
turns.zh: 好。赢家继续赢，这些产品？

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: Yeah. If anything, it's like when you don't talk about the SaaS products you use, I feel like that's more of a success because it's just, it works behind the scenes, it blends in and it just makes everyone so much more productive.
turns.zh: 对。如果你不谈你用的 SaaS，我觉得那更多是成功，因为它就在幕后运转、融入、让所有人更高效。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Imagine all these companies have the New York Times logo on their site of people using that.
turns.zh: 对。想象所有这些公司有纽约时报 logo 在用户那里。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: Maybe.
turns.zh: 也许。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That would be a big deal when you guys adopt a product. Final question. Who else in the industry do you most respect as a thought leader and thinker?
turns.zh: 你们采用一个产品会是大事。最后一个问题。业界你最尊敬谁作为 thought leader 和思考者？

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: This is a hard question, but I would say one of the people who I find to just be a really tremendous product thinker, leader, and ally for women is Fidji Simo. I was lucky enough to work with her and for her when I was at Facebook and just watching the way that she ... what she did with Facebook, what she then is doing at Instacart and the way that she really just helps so many other women in the field figure out how to be better at their craft, how to have more opportunity. I don't know how she has these many hours in her day, but she's pretty incredible, so I would love to give a shout out to her.
turns.zh: 这难。但我觉得一个我觉得是真正 tremendous 的产品思考者、leader 和女性盟友的是 Fidji Simo。我有幸在 Facebook 时和她共事、为她工作。看她做了什么——Facebook、然后 Instacart——以及她帮那么多女性 figure out 怎么做得更好、怎么有更多机会。我不知道她一天怎么有那么多小时，但她相当 incredible，我想给她 shout out。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. I will try to get her on this podcast.
turns.zh: 太好了。我会努力请她上播客。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: Oh, that would be amazing. All right. She's really-
turns.zh: 哦，那太棒了。好。她真的——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's what I need to do. Awesome. Good recommendation. Alex, this was amazing. I learned so much. This is such a fun conversation. Thank you, again, for doing this. Two last questions, where can folks find you online if they want to reach out and learn more? Maybe think about working at the New York Times and otherwise, how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 这就是我该做的。太好了。好推荐。Alex，这太棒了。我学了很多。这次对话很有趣。再次谢谢你。最后两个问题：大家想联系你、了解更多、也许想在纽约时报工作，在哪能找到你？然后听众怎么能帮到你？

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: Thanks. You can find me on Twitter, LinkedIn, all the usual channels. I would love to hear from anyone and would be delighted to also talk about what it's like to do product at the Times. Then, the thing that would be really useful is what is the one feature that would make the New York Times more essential and more valuable to you in your daily life? I would love to hear from people on that front.
turns.zh: 谢谢。你可以 Twitter、LinkedIn 等通常渠道找到我。我很乐意听任何人聊，也很乐意谈在纽约时报做产品是什么样。然后真正有用的是：什么一个功能能让纽约时报在你日常生活里更必备、更有价值？我很想听大家这方面。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: All right. I shared mine, a design-oriented Wirecutter. I will be looking for that.
turns.zh: 好。我分享了我的——设计导向的 Wirecutter。我会找那个。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: Thank you.
turns.zh: 谢谢。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Thank you, Alex.
turns.zh: 太好了。谢谢你 Alex。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: No, of course. There's just one other whole theme, and I don't know if you want to chat through it, which is, what are some of the similarities and differences between product management in news organization?
turns.zh: 不，当然。还有一个整个主题，不知道你想不想聊，就是新闻组织里产品管理的相似和不同？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's do it.
turns.zh: 来吧。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: It's totally up to you. But if that's something that you'd be interested in talking through.
turns.zh: 完全看你。如果你有兴趣聊的话。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Absolutely.
turns.zh: 绝对。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: I'm going to just focus on two themes that I think are pretty interesting. The first is just how we work at the New York Times, and we talked a little bit about working with journalism, and there are some really interesting differences. The second is just on the idea of impact. I think how the definition and the understanding of impact can be pretty different. First, just on the idea of how we work, there are a lot of similarities. I would say that product managers at the Times and at tech companies, they have a lot of the same skills. Like, we look for a great product sense, great execution, great leadership and drive.
turns.zh: 我只聚焦两个我觉得有意思的主题。第一是我们在纽约时报怎么工作，我们聊过一些和新闻合作，有一些很有趣的不同。第二是关于影响。影响的理解和定义可以很不同。先说怎么工作，有很多相似。纽约时报的 PM 和科技公司的 PM 有很多同样技能。我们找好的产品感、好的执行、好的领导力和驱动力。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: Any good PM needs to know their industry, their customers, their market, their business, et cetera. We actually do see a lot of crossover between product managers from tech companies who come to the New York Times or tech PMs at the Times who go over to tech companies. I think that that's wonderful, but a key difference of when you're a product manager working at the New York Times is that you work across the full stack of the product. Meaning, we own our journalism and our content. We own our distribution and we own our products. That's really different from working at a big tech platform. When I was at Facebook, we controlled the software and the distribution, but we didn't control the content.
turns.zh: 任何好 PM 需要了解行业、客户、市场、业务。我们确实看到很多交叉——科技公司 PM 来纽约时报、或纽约时报 tech PM 去科技公司。我觉得那很好，但在纽约时报做 PM 的关键不同是你跨产品全栈工作。意思是我们 own 我们的新闻和内容。我们 own 分发。我们 own 产品。这和在大型科技平台工作很不同。我在 Facebook 时我们控制软件和分发，但不控制内容。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: We had real limitations on understanding what was passing through. Was it high quality content, low quality content? It just led to, again, a lot of challenges that we already talked about. At the Times, when I think about how our best products are born, it's when you bring journalism and product lovers together. That means that PMs at the Times really need to understand the blend of art and science. They really need to value expert editorial judgment as they're also looking at individual KPIs, customer research and insights, et cetera. An interesting example, as I was trying to think about what would feel really different doing product at the Times compared to say Facebook is like, let's say you're at the product team and you're working on the home screen.
turns.zh: 我们对什么在通过有真实限制。是高质量还是低质量？这导致了很多我们聊过的挑战。在纽约时报，我们最好的产品怎么诞生的，是把新闻和产品爱好者聚一起。这意味着 PM 真的需要理解艺术和科学的结合。需要在看个人 KPI、客户研究和洞察时也重视专家编辑判断。一个有趣的例子——我想在纽约时报做产品和 Facebook 不同的是什么——比如你在产品团队做首页。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: We always start with expert editorial judgment to curate the most important and interesting stories. But on top of that, we're training algorithms on specific data sets, like editorial important scores that actually come from our journalists. What that allows us to do is actually scale editorial judgment to a large group of readers. Those algorithms, what I think is just really great is they're trained on editorial signal and then they can still work towards driving towards outcomes like reach, engagement, conversion, et cetera. That's just such a different way of thinking. When I was at Facebook and we were focused on news ranking and feed, all we could do was train pieces of in information based on an engagement outcome.
turns.zh: 我们总是从专家编辑判断开始 curate 最重要、最有趣的故事。但之上我们用特定数据集训算法，如来自记者的编辑重要性分数。这让我们能把编辑判断扩展到大量读者。那些算法我觉得很棒的是它们在编辑信号上训练，然后还能朝触达、参与、转化等结果驱动。这是很不同的思考方式。我在 Facebook 做新闻排序和 feed 时，我们只能基于参与结果训信息。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: We couldn't actually train it based on the quality of that piece of information itself. At the Times you get all, you have 2000 plus journalists and you're actually trying to structure their expertise into things that can actually translate into really great algorithmic decisioning, and that's just so different. No one else is really doing something in that space. Product managers are becoming very editorially minded and we're also getting editors to become more product minded. I just think that how we work there is so different and so unique. It's just a pretty fascinating part of, I think, how the sausage is made, if that makes sense.
turns.zh: 我们没法基于信息本身的质量训练。在纽约时报你有 2000 多记者，你在试图把他们的专长结构化成能转化成很好的算法决策的东西，这太不同了。没别人真的在做这个。PM 变得很有编辑头脑，我们也让编辑变得更有产品头脑。我们怎么工作真的不同、独特。我觉得这是香肠怎么做的一个相当迷人的部分，如果这说得通。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Thanks for sharing that. I think that's really important topic of just how it's different and why it's worth considering trying something like the New York Times as a place to work. What's interesting about what you're talking about, this also reminds me ironically of Substack, where they also are anti-algorithms and are also very focused on people and people recommending other people and just like individuals. I don't know if we want to get into this, but I guess do you have a opinion of Substack as a medium? Because folks leave New York Times to work on Substack, they come back. My whole living is on Substack. Any thoughts on the world of Substack?
turns.zh: 对。谢谢分享。我觉得这很重要：怎么不同、为什么值得考虑去纽约时报这种地方工作。有意思的是这也让我讽刺地想到 Substack，他们也反算法、非常聚焦人和人推荐人。我不知道想不想进这个，但你大概对 Substack 作为媒介有看法？因为有人离开纽约时报去 Substack、又回来。我整个生计在 Substack。对 Substack 的世界有什么想法？

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: Well, a couple of things. First, it's not that we're anti-algorithm on the New York Times front, it's just that we want our algorithms to reflect editorial judgment. That's really different. When it comes to Substack, actually, I think a lot of what Substack is doing is great. The idea of writers being able to make a living individually off of their craft, I think, is fantastic. The thing that I get excited about for Substack, but also for a company like the New York Times is trust right now with institutions has been declining, with governments, with religious institutions, with news organizations.
turns.zh: 几点。首先纽约时报不是反算法，我们只是要让算法反映编辑判断。那很不同。关于 Substack，其实我觉得 Substack 做的很多事很棒。写作者能靠 craft 个人谋生，我觉得 fantastic。让我兴奋的——对 Substack 也对纽约时报——是信任：对机构的信任在下降，对政府、宗教机构、新闻机构。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: But trust with individual experts, where you have a real relationship, that really matters. That I think is one of the big unlocks in terms of helping the next generation of readers really start to create more of a relationship with high quality journalists and writers who have really important things to say about the world. I think whatever is happening in the world that helps great writers find their audiences, make a living, is wonderful. At the New York Times, a lot of what we're trying to do is, it's not the Substack model, but we have a lot more that we're doing to actually help get individual journalists out there.
turns.zh: 但对个人专家、你有真实关系的，那种信任很重要。我觉得那是帮下一代读者和高质量记者、有重要话说的写作者建立关系的大解锁之一。我觉得世界上任何帮好写作者找到受众、谋生的事都很好。在纽约时报，我们试图做的很多——不是 Substack 模式——但我们做了很多让个人记者走出去。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: They have their own subscribe only newsletters, podcasts. We're really trying to help them find a way to create a mini platform within the means and the scale of the New York Times. It's not quite the Substack model, but I do think that there's some interesting similarities, and the more that artists and creatives can help make a living, I think, it's just fantastic.
turns.zh: 他们有自己的 subscribe-only newsletter、podcast。我们真的在帮他们找方式在纽约时报的资源和规模内创造 mini 平台。不太是 Substack 模式，但我觉得有些有趣相似，越多人能靠创作谋生就越棒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm here for it. I love this two-part encore bonus we just did. Anything else that you want to share before we wrap up?

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: I think the only other thing that I have come to learn when you're doing product management at a news organization compared to a place like Facebook is just how different the definition of impact can be. When I was at Facebook, we were incredibly focused on scale, engagement, and revenue, which is very appropriate. At a company like the New York Times, we also have a huge ambition to grow our subscriber base. But one thing that's really interesting is that our impact and our business goals are in service of our mission, which is to seek the truth and help people understand the world, not the other way around.
turns.zh: 我觉得在新闻组织做 PM 和在 Facebook 那种地方做的唯一其他学到的事是影响的定义可以多不同。在 Facebook 我们极度聚焦规模、参与和收入，这很合适。在纽约时报这种公司我们也有大雄心增长订阅者。但一件很有意思的事是我们的影响力和商业目标是为使命服务的，使命是寻求真相、帮人理解世界，不是反过来。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: What it means is that the way that we think about impact is growing a giant subscription business. That business exists to strengthen an informed democracy at a time when people are struggling to understand basic facts and struggling to understand each other. That means that impact for us is growing subscribers, but it's also when a deeply reported story triggers an important policy change or a new law. When you're a product manager you're involved, again, in driving specific metrics like engagement or subscribers.
turns.zh: 这意味着我们想影响的方式是壮大一个巨型订阅业务。那个业务的存在是为了在人们难以理解基本事实、难以相互理解的时代，强化一个知情的民主。所以影响对我们是增长订阅者，也是一篇深度报道触发重要政策改变或新法律。当你是 PM，你驱动参与或订阅者等具体指标。

turns.speaker: Alex Hardiman
turns.en: But you're also trying to help stories find their real audience in ways that trigger just this whole different side of mission and purpose driven impact. I didn't feel that when I was at a place like Facebook, but at the Times, I think it just gives product managers a bit of a broader aperture in the ways that they think about the relationship between business goals and mission impact goals, and it's pretty cool.
turns.zh: 但你也在帮故事找到真正受众，触发完全不同的使命和目的驱动的影响力。我在 Facebook 没感受到，但在纽约时报我觉得它给 PM 更宽的光圈去想商业目标和使命影响目标的关系，挺酷。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It does feel like it would be hard to find more meaningful, impactful work, and so that really resonates.
turns.zh: 确实感觉很难找到更有意义、更有影响的工作了，所以那真的很共鸣。

turns.en: Oh, thanks. There are so many other important purposeful products and problems out there to solve in the world. We need product managers everywhere diagnosing key problems and issues, coming up with radically novel solutions. This is the moment. It's really great to have your podcast and so many other resources out there to help new and other PMs just do their best craft. Thank you for having all of us in here.
